claim: The proportion of parents who experienced child loss decreased from 61.1% of those born 1800–1880 to 5.2% of those born after 1930.
source: The proportion of parents who experienced child loss decreased from 61.1% of those born 1800–1880 to 5.2% of those born after 1930.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data presented in the abstract and results section of the manuscript, showing specific percentages calculated from the genealogical database.

claim: Child loss was consistently associated with increased rate of maternal, but not paternal, death before the age of 50 across all parent birth cohorts.
source: Child loss was consistently associated with increased rate of maternal, but not paternal, death before the age of 50 across all parent birth cohorts
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in the results, including hazard ratios and confidence intervals shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: The relative increase in maternal mortality rate ranged from 35% among mothers born 1800–1930 to 64% among mothers born after 1930.
source: the relative increase in maternal mortality rate ranged from 35% among mothers born 1800–1930 to 64% among mothers born after 1930.
evidence: This claim is supported by hazard ratio calculations from the Cox proportional hazards models presented in the results section.

claim: Infant mortality rates in Iceland dropped from 238 per 1000 births in 1881–1885 to 2.07 in 2005–2010.
source: infant mortality rates in Iceland (per 1000 births) dropped from one of the highest known values in history, 238 in 1881–1885 (Jónsson and Magnússon, 1997), to one of the lowest, 2.07 in 2005–2010 (Statistics Iceland, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Jónsson and Magnússon, 1997; Statistics Iceland, 2019) that provide the specific infant mortality rate data.

claim: From 1817 to 2015, 64,044 parents lost at least one child.
source: From 1817 to 2015, 64 044 parents lost at least one child (Supplementary file 1 - Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data from the genealogical database analysis, with reference to a supplementary table.

claim: Parents who lost a child were more likely to be women compared to their siblings who did not lose a child.
source: Compared to their siblings who did not lose a child, parents who lost a child were more likely to be women, have more children, be younger at first childbirth and older at cohort entry, and have a longer follow-up time (p<0.05; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison data presented in Table 1, with p-values indicating statistical significance.

claim: Parents who lost a child had more children compared to their siblings who did not lose a child.
source: Compared to their siblings who did not lose a child, parents who lost a child were more likely to be women, have more children, be younger at first childbirth and older at cohort entry, and have a longer follow-up time (p<0.05; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison data presented in Table 1, showing mean number of children of 5.80 for parents with loss versus 4.21 for parents without loss.

claim: Parents who lost a child were younger at first childbirth compared to their siblings who did not lose a child.
source: Compared to their siblings who did not lose a child, parents who lost a child were more likely to be women, have more children, be younger at first childbirth and older at cohort entry, and have a longer follow-up time (p<0.05; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison data in Table 1, showing mean age at first childbirth of 25.55 years for parents with loss versus 27.16 years for parents without loss.

claim: Throughout the entire study period, there was an elevated hazard ratio of overall mortality rate among parents who lost a child (HR 1.04; 95% CI 1.02–1.06).
source: Throughout the entire study period, we observed an elevated hazard ratio (HR) of overall mortality rate among parents who lost a child (1.04; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02–1.06)
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards model analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The elevated mortality rate among parents who lost a child was mostly driven by maternal rather than paternal mortality rates.
source: which was mostly driven by maternal (HR 1.07; 95% CI 1.04–1.10) rather than paternal mortality rates (HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.99–1.05; p-for-difference=0.0096).
evidence: This claim is supported by sex-stratified Cox proportional hazards model results with statistical testing for difference between sexes.

claim: There was an increase in mortality rate after child loss for parents born after 1930 compared to parents born 1800–1930.
source: except for an increase in mortality rate after child loss for parents born after 1930 (p-for-difference = 0.002 when compared to parents born 1800–1930).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of hazard ratios across birth cohorts with a p-value indicating statistical significance.

claim: Before the age of 50, mothers who lost a child experienced increased mortality (HR 1.36; 95% CI 1.27–1.45) during the whole study period.
source: Before the age of 50, mothers who lost a child experienced increased mortality (HR 1.36; 95% CI 1.27–1.45) during the whole study period
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards model analysis restricted to follow-up before age 50, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The hazard ratios for maternal mortality before age 50 after child loss were consistently elevated across all seven birth cohorts.
source: with the HRs consistently elevated across all seven birth cohorts (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data visualization in Figure 2a showing hazard ratios for each birth cohort.

claim: No excess mortality was observed for fathers who lost a child in any of the birth cohorts before age 50 (HR for entire observation period 1.04; 95% CI 0.97–1.11).
source: In contrast, no such excess mortality was observed for fathers who lost a child in any of the birth cohorts (HR for entire observation period 1.04; 95% CI 0.97–1.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards model analysis for fathers, with confidence intervals crossing 1.0 indicating no statistically significant effect.

claim: The excess maternal mortality rates before the age of 50 after child loss seem limited to loss of a child younger than 18 years.
source: the excess maternal mortality rates before the age of 50 after child loss seem limited to loss of a child younger than 18 years, while the elevation in paternal mortality rates are more notable after loss of an adult child (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by subgroup analysis by child's age at loss presented in Table 2.

claim: The elevation in paternal mortality rates before age 50 are more notable after loss of an adult child.
source: the excess maternal mortality rates before the age of 50 after child loss seem limited to loss of a child younger than 18 years, while the elevation in paternal mortality rates are more notable after loss of an adult child (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by subgroup analysis by child's age at loss presented in Table 2, showing HR 1.99 (95% CI 1.24–3.20) for fathers losing children aged 18+.

claim: Loss of infants represented 59% of child losses during the study period.
source: The difference between mothers and fathers in excess mortality rate before the age of 50 is particularly marked after loss of infants, representing 59% of child losses during the study period.
evidence: This claim is supported by descriptive statistics from the genealogical database analysis.

claim: After the age of 50 and across the entire study period, neither mothers (HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.99–1.05) nor fathers (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.98–1.05) suffered increased mortality rate after child loss.
source: After the age of 50 and across the entire study period, neither mothers (HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.99–1.05) nor fathers (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.98–1.05) suffered increased mortality rate after child loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards model analysis restricted to follow-up after age 50.

claim: Parents older than 50 who lost a child and were born after 1930 experienced significantly increased mortality (HR 1.11; 95% CI 1.03–1.20; p=0.0063).
source: we observed significantly increased mortality in parents older than 50 who lost a child and were born after 1930 (HR 1.11; 95% CI 1.03–1.20; p=0.0063), particularly among fathers (HR 1.21; 95% CI 1.08–1.37; p=0.0009; Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by subgroup analysis by birth cohort for parents over age 50, as shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The recent increase in mortality after the age of 50 years is associated with child loss that mostly occurred before the age of 50.
source: this recent increase in mortality after the age of 50 years is associated with child loss that mostly occurred before the age of 50 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of timing of child loss relative to parent age, presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The deCODE Genetics genealogy database contains information on kinship, dates of birth and death of Icelandic population largely since settlement.
source: The data source for the current study is the deCODE Genetics genealogy database, containing information on kinship, dates of birth and death of Icelandic population largely since settlement (Gudbjartsson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a publication describing the database (Gudbjartsson et al., 2015).

claim: The genealogical database contains an almost complete record of the ancestors of contemporary Icelanders back to around 1650.
source: The database contains an almost complete record of the ancestors of contemporary Icelanders back to around 1650
evidence: This claim describes a characteristic of the database used in the study.

claim: After 1880, the genealogical database is based on death records from a geographically comprehensive set of parish records.
source: after 1880, is based on death records from a geographically comprehensive set of parish records.
evidence: This claim describes the data sources used to construct the genealogical database.

claim: The completeness of the genealogical database across the entire observation period is 99% in terms of linkages between parents and offspring.
source: In terms of linkages between parents and offspring, the completeness of the genealogical database across the entire observation period is 99%.
evidence: This claim provides a data quality metric for the genealogical database.

claim: The database has been extensively evaluated for the accuracy of linkage using genetic data.
source: The database has been extensively evaluated for the accuracy of such linkage using genetic data (Sun et al., 2012; Helgason et al., 2015; Halldorsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to publications that validated the database using genetic data.

claim: 323,510 individuals born from January 1st 1800 through December 31st 1996 and living in Iceland were eligible for inclusion in the study.
source: In total 323,510 individuals were eligible for inclusion
evidence: This claim provides the initial sample size for the study based on inclusion criteria.

claim: 27,704 individuals who emigrated after 1906 were not included in the study population.
source: 27,704 individuals who emigrated after 1906 were not included in the study population.
evidence: This claim describes an exclusion criterion applied to the study population.

claim: 12,233 (3.8%) parents who were lost to follow-up were excluded from the study.
source: We excluded 12,233 (3.8%) parents who were lost to follow-up.
evidence: This claim provides information about attrition in the study cohort.

claim: The death of a child is arguably one of the most stressful events that a parent can experience.
source: The death of a child is arguably one of the most stressful events that a parent can experience.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of psychology and stress research.

claim: Grief has been described across human populations.
source: Grief is the natural emotional response to such loss and has been described across human populations (Lindemann, 1944; Bowlby, 1980; Parkes, 2014; Boyden et al., 2014; Einarsdóttir, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on grief across different populations.

claim: Child loss has been associated with elevated risks of psychiatric symptoms.
source: Thus, child loss has been associated with elevated risks of psychiatric symptoms (Kreicbergs et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on psychiatric symptoms after child loss.

claim: Child loss has been associated with psychiatric hospitalizations.
source: psychiatric hospitalizations (Li et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on psychiatric hospitalizations after child loss.

claim: Child loss has been associated with sickness absence.
source: sickness absence (Wilcox et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on sickness absence after child loss.

claim: Child loss has been associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: cardiovascular disease (Li et al., 2002a; Li et al., 2003a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cardiovascular disease after child loss.

claim: Child loss has been associated with some cancers.
source: and some cancers (Fang et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2013; Li et al., 2002b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cancer risk after child loss.

claim: Parents, particularly mothers, who lose a child face increased risk of death.
source: Studies also suggest that parents, particularly mothers, who lose a child face increased risk of death (Li et al., 2002a; Li et al., 2003a; Levav et al., 1988; Li et al., 2003b; Qin and Mortensen, 2003; Agerbo, 2005; Rostila et al., 2012; Rostila et al., 2015; Espinosa and Evans, 2013; Harper et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Schorr et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on parental mortality after child loss.

claim: Parents who lose a child face increased risk of death both from suicide and natural causes.
source: both from suicide and natural causes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the preceding citations to studies on parental mortality after child loss.

claim: Previous studies on child loss and parent mortality were all conducted in affluent developed populations where infant mortality rates are low and life expectancy is high.
source: The aforementioned studies were all conducted in affluent developed populations, where infant mortality rates are low and life expectancy is high.
evidence: This claim characterizes the existing literature on child loss and parent mortality.

claim: In contemporary developing nations, infant mortality rates >50 per 1000 live births are common.
source: In contemporary developing nations, infant mortality rates (number of deaths during first year per 1000 live births) >50 are common
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to United Nations data on infant mortality rates.

claim: In developed nations, infant mortality rates are usually lower than eight per 1000 live births.
source: whereas in developed nations they are usually lower than eight (United Nations, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to United Nations data on infant mortality rates.

claim: Some historians argue for parental reluctance to invest emotions in children where mortality rates are high.
source: Parent-child attachment in pre-industrial and developing populations has been a matter of debate, with some historians arguing for parental reluctance to invest emotions in children where mortality rates are high
evidence: This claim describes a historical debate in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Some historians argue that parents' attachment and grief after child loss is similar across human populations, past and present.
source: while others argue that parents' attachment and grief after child loss is similar across human populations, past and present (Magnússon, 2010; Woods, 2003).
evidence: This claim describes an alternative view in the historical debate, supported by citations.

claim: The study followed all Icelandic parents born 1800 or later from the birth of their first child (earliest from 1817) until death or to the end of 2015.
source: We followed all Icelandic parents, born 1800 or later, from the birth of their first child (earliest from 1817) until death or to the end of 2015
evidence: This claim describes the study design and follow-up period.

claim: The primary analyses were focused on the 47,711 parents who lost a child and had at least one sibling who did not lose a child (N = 126,342).
source: our primary analyses were focused on the 47,711 parents who lost a child and had at least one sibling who did not lose a child (N = 126,342).
evidence: This claim describes the primary analytical cohort used in the study.

claim: The sibling-controlled design was used to adjust for potential confounding by socioeconomic status or other familial factors that might affect the risk of mortality.
source: To adjust for potential confounding by socioeconomic status or other familial factors that might affect the risk of mortality, our primary analyses were focused on the 47,711 parents who lost a child and had at least one sibling who did not lose a child (N = 126,342).
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for the sibling-controlled study design.

claim: Among 64,044 parents with loss, 54,532 (85.1%) had at least one sibling defined as sharing the same biological mother.
source: Among 64,044 parents with loss, 54,532 (85.1%) had at least one sibling defined as sharing the same biological mother.
evidence: This claim provides information about the proportion of exposed parents who could be matched to siblings.

claim: 6,821 parents were excluded because they only had siblings who had experienced child loss.
source: whereas 6821 parents were excluded because they only had siblings who had experienced child loss.
evidence: This claim describes an exclusion criterion for the sibling-based cohort.

claim: The results were robust to the exclusion of mothers who died within a week after giving birth.
source: These results were robust to the exclusion of mothers who died within a week after giving birth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The higher mortality rate in mothers after child loss is unlikely to be explained by delivery or postpartum complications that resulted in the deaths of both newborn and mother.
source: making it unlikely that the higher mortality rate in mothers is explained by delivery or postpartum complications that resulted in the deaths of both newborn and mother (Nour, 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the sensitivity analysis excluding mothers who died within a week after giving birth, combined with knowledge about postpartum complications.

claim: The recent increase in parent mortality rate after the age of 50 may be due to an increased risk of long-term social isolation after child loss.
source: As a result, we postulate that the recent increase in parent mortality rate after the age of 50, particularly in fathers, may be due to an increased risk of long-term social isolation after child loss.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as a postulation (speculation) by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Very high mortality rates were found for parents born after 1930 who lost a child and had no living children at the age of 50.
source: In support of this notion, we indeed found very high mortality rates for parents born after 1930 who lost a child and had no living children at the age of 50, regardless of the sex of deceased child (Supplementary file 1 - Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1 - Table 4.

claim: The large increase in the rate of premature maternal mortality after child loss in 19th century Iceland suggests that mothers formed strong emotional bonds with their children in spite of very harsh conditions and a strong expectation of child loss.
source: The large increase in the rate of premature maternal mortality after child loss in 19th century Iceland suggests that mothers formed strong emotional bonds with their children – in spite of very harsh conditions and a strong expectation of child loss.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn by the authors from their findings about maternal mortality rates in 19th century Iceland.

claim: The findings are consistent with accounts of intense grieving among mothers who lost a child in a contemporary developing society.
source: This is consistent with accounts of intense grieving among mothers who lost a child in a contemporary developing society (Einarsdóttir, 2004).
evidence: This claim connects the study findings to previous ethnographic research, supported by citation.

claim: The paternal mortality response to child loss is much weaker throughout the observation period and only statistically significant for older fathers (i.e. parent mortality after 50 years of age) born after 1930.
source: In contrast, the paternal mortality response to child loss is much weaker throughout the observation period and only statistically significant for older fathers (i.e. parent mortality after 50 years of age) born after 1930.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings for fathers across the study period.

claim: Throughout the 199-year study period, mothers may have had greater opportunity than fathers to form early emotional attachment to their infants through gestation and breastfeeding.
source: Throughout the 199-year study period, mothers may have had greater opportunity than fathers to form early emotional attachment to their infants through gestation and breastfeeding.
evidence: This claim is a speculative explanation offered by the authors for the sex difference in mortality response.

claim: Breastfeeding may have been rarer in 19th to early 20th century Iceland than in the present.
source: Although historical accounts suggest that breastfeeding may have been rarer in 19th to early 20th century Iceland (Garðarsdóttir, 2005) than in the present
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical research on breastfeeding practices in Iceland.

claim: It is possible that females are born with a tendency to form stronger emotional bonds with children than males.
source: It is possible that females are born with a tendency to form stronger emotional bonds with children than males.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as a possibility (speculation) by the authors.

claim: The mortality response of fathers to child loss before the age of 50 has not significantly increased despite the greater contribution of fathers to the postnatal care of children in recent decades.
source: it is interesting to note that the mortality response of fathers to child loss before the age of 50 has not significantly increased despite the greater contribution of fathers to the postnatal care of children in recent decades (Huerta et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim combines findings from the study with knowledge about changing paternal roles, supported by citation.

claim: Women have been reported to have a greater risk of mental disorders after exposure to emotional trauma than men.
source: Women have been reported to have a greater risk of mental disorders after exposure to emotional trauma than men (Tolin and Foa, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on sex differences in response to trauma.

claim: Previous studies in contemporary developed populations have reported evidence for greater risk of psychiatric hospitalizations after child loss in mothers than in fathers.
source: Previous studies in contemporary developed populations have reported evidence for greater risk of psychiatric hospitalizations (Li et al., 2005) and mortality (Li et al., 2003b) after child loss in mothers than in fathers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on sex differences in outcomes after child loss.

claim: Previous studies in contemporary developed populations have reported evidence for greater risk of mortality after child loss in mothers than in fathers.
source: Previous studies in contemporary developed populations have reported evidence for greater risk of psychiatric hospitalizations (Li et al., 2005) and mortality (Li et al., 2003b) after child loss in mothers than in fathers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on sex differences in outcomes after child loss.

claim: An opposite sex difference is seen for mortality rate after spousal loss, where mortality rate elevation is more pronounced among widowers than widows.
source: Interestingly, an opposite sex difference is seen for mortality rate after spousal loss, where mortality rate elevation is more pronounced among widowers than widows (Moon et al., 2011; Shor et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on mortality after spousal loss.

claim: The sex difference in mortality after spousal loss may in part be due to a greater dependence of older males on social and emotional support provided by spouses.
source: However, this difference may in part be due to a greater dependence of older males on social and emotional support provided by spouses.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation offered by the authors to explain the sex difference in mortality after spousal loss.

claim: Child loss is likely to constitute a major threat to the survival of mothers in societies with high infant mortality rates.
source: Indeed, one implication of our findings is that child loss is likely to constitute a major threat to the survival of mothers in societies with high infant mortality rates.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn by the authors from their findings, extending the implications to other societies.

claim: The findings contradict claims that mothers in poor cultures adapt to high infant mortality rates with reduced emotional investment.
source: This contradicts claims that mothers in poor cultures adapt to high infant mortality rates with reduced emotional investment (as reviewed in Woods, 2003).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn by the authors, contrasting their findings with a theory in the literature.

claim: The study has no information about the causes of death for children or parents.
source: First, we have no information about the causes of death for children or parents.
evidence: This claim is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Some impact of reverse causation, for example the ill-health of parents increasing the mortality risk of their children, cannot be ruled out.
source: Some impact of reverse causation, for example the ill-health of parents increasing the mortality risk of their children, cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This claim is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding potential reverse causation.

claim: The relatively stable effect estimates of parent mortality rates after child loss across calendar periods argues against a strong influence of reverse causality.
source: The relatively stable effect estimates of parent mortality rates after child loss across calendar periods and the consistently lower impact of child loss on paternal mortality argues against a strong influence of reverse causality.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn by the authors from the pattern of their results.

claim: The consistently lower impact of child loss on paternal mortality argues against a strong influence of reverse causality.
source: The relatively stable effect estimates of parent mortality rates after child loss across calendar periods and the consistently lower impact of child loss on paternal mortality argues against a strong influence of reverse causality.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn by the authors from the pattern of their results.

claim: The study did not have direct information about the socioeconomic status of parents.
source: Second, we did not have direct information about the socioeconomic status of parents.
evidence: This claim is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The sibling-controlled analysis is likely to adjust for much of the confounding due to socioeconomic status.
source: However, as socioeconomic status tends to cluster in families, our sibling-controlled analysis is likely to adjust for much of the confounding due to this source.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the effectiveness of the sibling-controlled design in addressing confounding.

claim: It is possible that the fragmented registration of births in earlier times resulted in misclassification of some parents who had truly lost a child.
source: Third, it is possible that the fragmented registration of births in earlier times (particularly in the case of infant deaths) resulted in misclassification of some parents who had truly lost a child
evidence: This claim is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding potential misclassification.

claim: Misclassification due to fragmented registration would result in somewhat conservative estimates of excess parent mortality rates in earlier times.
source: and, thus, somewhat conservative estimates of excess parent mortality rates in earlier times.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the direction of bias from potential misclassification.

claim: Parents who lost a child may have to live longer to experience such an event, which could introduce survivor bias.
source: Indeed, parents who lost a child may have to live longer to experience such an event, however, such survivor bias (if any) due to a selection of survivors to the exposed group would rather yield conservative estimates of parent mortality after a child loss.
evidence: This claim is a discussion of potential survivor bias and its direction of effect.

claim: Survivor bias due to selection of survivors to the exposed group would yield conservative estimates of parent mortality after child loss.
source: however, such survivor bias (if any) due to a selection of survivors to the exposed group would rather yield conservative estimates of parent mortality after a child loss.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the direction of bias from potential survivor bias.

claim: Siblings used for comparison that were not yet parents at the age when the index parents lost a child may have a survival advantage.
source: On the other hand, the siblings used for comparison that were not yet parents at the age as when the index parents lost a child may have a survival advantage
evidence: This claim is a discussion of potential bias in the comparison group.

claim: A survival advantage in comparison siblings could yield exaggerated estimates of parent mortality after child loss.
source: which could yield exaggerated estimates of parent mortality after child loss.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the direction of bias from potential survival advantage in comparison siblings.

claim: Similar results were observed in a sensitivity analysis restricted to unexposed siblings who were already parents at the same age as when the index parents lost a child.
source: However, we observed similar results in a sensitivity analysis that was restricted to unexposed siblings who were already parents at the same age as when the index parents lost a child.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results addressing potential bias from comparison siblings.

claim: The study period spans two centuries of drastic demographic transition in Iceland, from a poor developing nation with a particularly high infant mortality rate, to a modern affluent nation with one of the lowest rates of infant mortality in history.
source: The study period spans two centuries of drastic demographic transition in Iceland, from a poor developing nation with a particularly high infant mortality rate, to a modern affluent nation with one of the lowest rates of infant mortality in history.
evidence: This claim summarizes the historical context of the study period.

claim: The most striking finding is the consistent increase in premature maternal deaths in response to child loss throughout the 199 years of observation.
source: the most striking finding is the consistent increase in premature maternal deaths in response to child loss throughout the 199 years of observation.
evidence: This claim is the authors' interpretation of their most important finding.

claim: The study leverages a unique nationwide data source of genealogies with virtually complete follow-up over a 199 year period spanning an extreme change in indicators of societal development.
source: This study leverages a unique nationwide data source of genealogies with virtually complete follow-up over a 199 year period spanning an extreme change in indicators of societal development, for example infant and child mortality rate.
evidence: This claim describes a key strength of the study.

claim: Conditional Cox proportional hazards models were used to contrast the mortality rates of parents who lost at least one child to their respective siblings who did not.
source: We used a conditional Cox proportional hazards model to contrast the mortality rates of parents who lost at least one child to their respective siblings who did not (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim describes the primary statistical method used in the analysis.

claim: The hazard ratios changed minimally after exclusion of parent-child pairs with the same date of death.
source: The HRs changed minimally after exclusion of parent-child pairs with the same date of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar results were obtained from the population-based matched cohort and a subset of this cohort with identifiable siblings, separately.
source: Similar results were obtained from the population-based matched cohort and a subset of this cohort with identifiable siblings, separately, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of results across different analytical approaches shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Greater hazard ratios were observed in the population-based matched cohort compared to the sibling-controlled cohort, revealing the importance of the sibling-controlled design to adjust for unmeasured familial confounding factors.
source: albeit with greater HRs revealing the importance of the sibling-controlled design to adjust for unmeasured familial confounding factors.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from comparing results between different analytical approaches.
